content:
Hi all, everyone who's ever used mathlib's API for Weierstrass elliptic curves (including myself) has at some point\* complained about the four definitions WeierstrassCurve and WeierstrassCurve.Affine/Projective/Jacobian (which are in fact type synonyms of each other!). I introduced these in 2024 as a hack for dot notation to avoid name clashes (WeierstrassCurve.Affine/Projective/Jacobian.Equation/Nonsingular/Point), but this has clearly proven to be more annoying than helpful. A few months ago @Thomas Browning suggested that we should have one publicly-visible point type, and everything else should be implementation details. I've been doing a large experiment (with the help of Claude) to refactor the entire library, trying to balance proofs and computations. I've come up with a design in a private repository that I'm pretty satisfied with, but I'd like to listen to the community's opinions before I start making PRs. Everything I say here will be under the namespace WeierstrassCurve for simplicity.

The first point\* of departure is that the default coordinate system will be projective, and not affine like what it is currently. You can have a look at the existing projective API to see how it works, but the point\* is that a point on an arbitrary Weierstrass curve W over an arbitrary commutative ring R is represented by a triple (x:y:z) of elements in R, such that the ideal (x,y,z) is R, up to simultaneous multiplication by units as in the post by @Junyan Xu. The proposition that it lies on the curve will be called OnCurveₚ (so we can say W.OnCurveₚ P), which replaces the existing Affine/Projective/Jacobian.Equation that didn't satisfy mathlib naming conventions. Maybe someone can suggest a better name?

The Point type will be a structure with these two fields, which is the second point\* of departure: this is different from the current Affine.Point, because we include singular points. As discussed in the post by @Junyan Xu, there will be a NonsingularPoint (or Pointₙₛ or Point₀), which just extends this with a condition Point.IsNonsingularₚ (or IsNonsingularₚ) that the ideal generated by its partial derivatives is R. Note that this is completely decoupled from OnCurveₚ, unlike now. The API will still mostly be about NonsingularPoint, which can be passed to Point when W.IsElliptic since the forgetful map NonsingularPoint → Point will be a bijection. There will also be an IsSingularₚ (or Point.IsSingularₚ) saying the partial derivatives all vanish, which is not always the negation of IsNonsingularₚ when R is not a field, but the corresponding structure SingularPoint extends Point is always a subsingleton over a reduced ring (or even unique when R is a perfect field, see the PR by @Andrew Yang).

The affine and Jacobian coordinates haven't disappeared! With some meta hacks, I could make it so that it's (hopefully) equally convenient to print/check/eval/compute/prove with any of the three coordinate systems. Instead of explaining what I did, I'll just show how it could work.

def E : WeierstrassCurve (ZMod 8) := ⟨1, 0, 0, 0, 1⟩ -- `y² + xy = x³ + 1` over a local ring `ℤ/2³ℤ`
instance : E.IsElliptic := ⟨by decide +kernel⟩ -- it's an elliptic curve, so `E.Point` is a group

-- there are autoParams `by first | assumption | decide +kernel` to prove `OnCurveₚ`
example : E.Point := ⟮1,1⟯ -- affine, secretly projective
example : E.Point := [3:3:3] -- projective
example : E.Point := [1;3;3] -- Jacobian, secretly projective
example : E.Point := ⟮1,2⟯ -- not on the curve, so gives an error

-- `#check` pretty prints the original coordinates
#check (⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point)   -- ⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point
#check ([3:3:3] : E.Point) -- [3:3:3] : E.Point
#check ([1;3;3] : E.Point) -- [1;3;3] : E.Point
#check (0 : E.Point) -- 0 : E.Point

-- `#eval` computes a "canonical form" whenever possible (field or finite ring), and as is otherwise
#eval ([3:3:3] : E.Point) -- normalise by a unit coordinate, prints affine ⟮1,1⟯
#eval ([1;3;3] : E.Point) -- same point, prints affine ⟮1,1⟯
#eval ([0:3:0] : E.Point) -- "the" point at infinity, prints 0
#eval ([6:3:0] : E.Point) -- a "different" point at infinity, prints [2:1:0]

-- the group law is computable, and you can even mix coordinates
#eval -(⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point) -- ⟮1,6⟯
#eval (⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point) + [2:1:0] -- ⟮7,1⟯
#eval (2 • ⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point) -- ⟮0,5⟯
#eval (4 • ⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point) -- [6:1:0]
#eval (8 • ⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point) -- 0
#eval Fintype.card E.Point -- 16

-- equality is decidable, and you can even mix coordinates
example : ([1;3;3] : E.Point) = ⟮1,1⟯ := by decide +kernel
example : ([0:5:0] : E.Point) = 0 := by decide +kernel
example : (4 • ⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point) = [6:1:0] := by decide +kernel
example : (8 • ⟮1,1⟯ : E.Point) = 0 := by decide +kernel

I think having a default coordinate system for Point is inevitable, but there is a very good point\* in choosing projective coordinates: we can have a group law over an arbitrary local ring! One of the addition laws already exists in mathlib (albeit absolutely horrendous), and can be heavily simplified with the corrections/simplifications of the Bosma--Lenstra formulae by @Junyan Xu. The group axioms (i.e. associativity) over local rings can be proven by transferring the affine group law through universal identities, without the need for any gluing or projective schemes. Over an arbitrary ring this will never work, but having it over local rings is sufficient to define things like the reduction homomorphism over local fields.

There is one annoying point\* that you may have noticed: OnCurve has a little subscript p, which is meant to suggest "projective". I still don't know the best way to handle duplicated names, so my current solution is to have subscripts a/p/j (thanks to a Lean 4 PR) instead of namespaces Affine/Projective/Jacobian. For instance, the notations ⟮1,1⟯/[3:3:3]/[1;3;3] are secretly just Point.mk constructors Point.mkₐ/ₚ/ⱼ. For proofs, instead of using cases/rcases/obtain, you'd use induction P using Point.casesOnₐ with | zero => ... | mkₐ x y h => ... for fields, induction P using Point.casesOnₚ with | mkₚ x y z h h' => ... for rings, and induction P using Point.casesOnⱼ with | mkⱼ x y z h h' => ... for local rings. This solution, which I call (0), means that there are almost 1000 declarations with subscripts, which might be annoying.

There are several alternative solutions:

  • (1) set a default coordinate system (not necessarily projective), but still have 500--700 declarations with subscripts for the other two,
  • (2) keep the namespaces Affine/Projective/Jacobian, but we can't use dot notation anymore,
  • (3) append the coordinate names (e.g. OnAffineCurve, IsProjectiveNonsingular, JacobianAddXYZ), which makes everything much longer, or
  • (4) add type synonyms for the point instead of the curve (e.g. W.OnCurve (p : AffineRep R) where AffineRep R is just R × R and W.IsNonsingular (P : ProjectiveRep R) where ProjectiveRep is just Fin 3 → R), but I see a tonne of ambiguous overloading problems here.

Any opinions and suggestions would be appreciated! What do you want to see in the API of elliptic curves?

\* pun totally intended

Projective coordinates sounds like a great default to me! As I'm sure you know, the definition of projective points which you propose above is "wrong" for an elliptic curve over a non-local ring, and I trust that you will flag this explicitly in the docstring. The reason I'm not worried too much about this is that the definition of elliptic curve itself is also "wrong" (but useful) over a general non-local ring (as is explicitly flagged in the docstring).
I don't know the maths but subscripts for name deduplication sounds fine to me! We do it all the time for Group vs GroupWithZero -based theorems, after all.

There is the worry that subscript a for affine "soft clashes" with (i.e. reminds people of, even though it has nothing to do with) AlgHom, or that the subscript 0 for nonsingular "soft clashes" with GroupWithZero, which is why I'm making this post to ask.

It would be reasonable to use Point for nonsingular points (as we're doing now) and Point₀ for all points, since if there's a unique singular point S then it is the absorbing "zero" element so that S + P = S for all nonsingular points P (however, S + S is not defined; I believe addition can only be extended to a morphism on Point × Point \ {(S,S)}, and this restrict to an action on Point₀ by Point).

Two issues with that: Point could be misleading (if it isn't already) and Point₀ was meant to imitate the subgroup E₀ of points with nonsingular reduction in the context of local fields, but yes otherwise you make a good point \*

David Ang said:

  • (3) append the coordinate names (e.g. OnAffineCurve, IsProjectiveNonsingular, JacobianAddXYZ), which makes everything much longer, or

Not my end of the library, but this would be my suggestion, with the small modification that you come up with a consistent place to put the adjective so that it doesn't need to be bikeshed for every declaration.
If you go with subscripts, then it definitely deserves a library note.
I just found Kevin's PR to the phrasebook by accident and realised how bad the current API is...
If you want more data points for how good/bad the API is, here is my experience of using it https://github.com/wwylele/Poncelet/blob/master/Poncelet/Elliptic.lean

David feel free to use that material in any way you like, I was quite pleased with the PR but apparently it was the wrong style for the phrasebook. It was written during a tutorial session for the phrasebook which was run by Anne, and my conclusion was that I had not properly understood what I was being taught in the tutorial because I had not written it in the right style.
Seems I also don’t understand the style!
